transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-19 15:30 PT
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Diego Marquez (Redwood SE), Arjun Patel (Skylark CTO), Maya Chen (Skylark ML Eng Lead), Tom Brooks (Skylark SRE)

Summary:
Skylark is evaluating Redwood for latency-sensitive streaming and high-concurrency throughput for their real-time summarization feature. Primary goals: p95 <= 350ms for 1-2k token streams, plan for bursts up to 50k tokens/sec aggregated, decision between hosted vs dedicated vs private given compliance and network constraints. Team agreed to run a token/sec benchmark with Redwood's harness and a dedicated capacity cost/options write-up.

Topics covered:
- p95 targets and how tokens/sec maps to concurrency and batching
- streaming latency tradeoffs vs throughput economics
- Dedicated pools vs Hosted auto-fallback and private VPC considerations
- Measurement methodology (prefix caching, KV cache impact, sequence length distribution)
- Security: SOC2, SSO, KMS, network egress
- Next steps: benchmark, cost estimate, follow-up deep bench session

Action items (captured in metadata above).

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'll run the meeting, Diego will jump in for the deep perf bits. Can you quickly state roles?
[00:07] Arjun (Skylark): Arjun Patel, CTO, we own the production infra for the summarization microservices.
[00:12] Maya (Skylark): Maya Chen, leads ML infra and latency optimizations.
[00:15] Tom (Skylark): Tom Brooks, SRE, I look after network and capacity.
[00:20] Diego (Redwood): Hey all. Quick agenda: p95 targets, current infra, constraints, and then tradeoffs hosted/dedicated/private.
[00:28] Arjun: Sounds good. High level: our user-facing summarizer is real-time. Average reply length is 250 tokens, but we stream partial results. We care most about p95 latency on token emission and we see bursts during peak office hours where tokens/sec spikes.
[00:40] Lena: Perfect — what's your current p95 and what are target numbers?
[00:44] Maya: Right now with our in-house distil model we see p95 of ~420ms for token chunks at 6 concurrent sessions per server. We want to get that under 350ms p95 for the next release. For throughput, our peak burst is around 40k tokens/sec across region, sustained is closer to 6-8k.
[01:05] Tom: Also, networking: we're in AWS us-west-2, and we have strict egress policies; anything that needs to talk out needs an allowlist and audit.
[01:13] Diego: Ok, clear. A few things to call out: p95 on streaming isn't just model latency — there is network, batching delay, and prefix/KV cache warmup. For streaming token emission we aim for per-token tail-latency control and continuous batching tuned to your sequence length distribution.
[01:30] Arjun: When you say batching, is that automatic on Redwood hosted? Or do we manage it?
[01:34] Diego: By default we run workload-aware batching in the runtime. It adapts to request arrival patterns. For hosted we control kernel selection and batching policies; for dedicated you get reserved pools where you can also set stricter SLOs and reduce cross-tenant variance.
[01:46] Maya: How much does batching add to p95? If we batch aggressively to increase throughput, won't that add latency to the first token?
[01:53] Diego: Great question. There's a tradeoff. The runtime uses adaptive thresholds — small micro-batches for low load, and larger batching during sustained throughput. For streaming we prioritize first-token latency by gating batch windows; during bursts we switch to a lower latency profile at cost of GPU utilization.
[02:09] Lena: Important for us — Skylark wants predictable p95 for SLAs. So can Redwood guarantee p95s for hosted?
[02:16] Diego: Hosted typically provides best-effort with documented performance profiles. For SLA-backed p95 commitments, Dedicated is the path: reserved GPU pools, capacity guarantees, and can config autoscale/burst. We also support private deployments if data residency or network constraints require it.
[02:31] Arjun: If we go dedicated, do we keep the same API and console? We don't want to rewrite client code.
[02:36] Lena: Yes — same API/console across hosted/dedicated/private. It's a key Redwood differentiator.
[02:41] Maya: On quantization: we run quantized variants — do you support int8 paths for streaming too?
[02:46] Diego: We do. Quantization reduces memory and can increase throughput but may slightly affect token emission timing depending on kernel paths. We'll give you a model-by-model profile.
[02:56] Tom: Security wise, SOC2 and SSO are table stakes. For private, can we bring our KMS?
[03:02] Lena: Yes, private deployments support customer-managed KMS/HSM integration and audit logs.
[03:07] Arjun: Great. Let's dig into the numbers — how do tokens/sec translate to GPU count and p95?
[03:12] Diego: Ok, quick back-of-envelope: it depends on model family, sequence length, and degree of streaming. For example, a 13B quantized model with typical 250-token responses and streaming can do X tokens/sec per A100-class GPU under our optimized kernel stack; with batching you'll amortize per-token cost. But I want to underline: it's workload-specific so we'll run an empirical benchmark.
[03:34] Maya: Can you give a rough multiplier? If we need to support bursts to 50k tokens/sec, do we need 10 GPUs or 50 GPUs?
[03:40] Diego: Very rough: with heavy streaming and small micro-batches, you might see ~3-6k tokens/sec per GPU on that config; so for a 50k burst you'd be looking at ~10-20 GPUs; but with larger batching and less strict first-token latency you could increase tokens/sec per GPU. We'll test against your prompt set.
[03:58] Arjun: Is there a built-in fallback if dedicated capacity is exhausted? We can't have a hard outage during bursts.
[04:03] Diego: Yes — smart routing can fallback to compatible hosted variants or other regions; you can set automatic fallback policies with cost/latency knobs. There are also burst bands in Dedicated to handle short peaks.
[04:15] Tom: For the fallback to hosted, does traffic route over public internet? We're worried about egress.
[04:20] Lena: For enterprise customers we offer VPC peering and private links for hosted failovers; private deployments avoid egress entirely. We'll capture your network requirements in the next steps.
[04:31] Maya: About measurement: we want p95 for token emission, but also p95 for first-byte and end-to-end generation. Which should we measure?
[04:40] Diego: We recommend measuring multiple: first-token latency (server and network), p95 token emission rate during stream, and end-to-end completion. Our benchmark harness will capture all three and show distribution plots.
[04:51] Arjun: What's the typical noise from KV cache warmup? We have a lot of repeated prefixes in queries.
[04:56] Diego: KV/prefix caching can significantly improve steady-state latency; warmup affects initial requests. We'll include warmup runs in the bench plan and measure cold vs warm p95.
[05:07] Maya: Any gotchas with TLS and TLS termination that add 50-80ms?
[05:12] Diego: TLS and networking stack do add tail latency; for low single-digit ms targets you'll need to account for your edge proxies. We can run tests through your infra or via our private link to isolate model runtime latency.
[05:25] Arjun: Okay. For benchmarking, what do you need from us?
[05:28] Lena: We'll need a representative prompt set, your desired p95 targets, examples of typical sequence length distribution, and network constraints. We'll provide a harness that can replay arrival patterns and measure token/sec and p95.
[05:40] Tom: We'll prepare that. One more — can Redwood run a latency-sensitivity mode where batching window is minimized?
[05:46] Diego: Yes, we can configure the runtime to use low-latency mode with more elastic GPU usage and potentially higher cost. We'll note that in the cost write-up.
[05:56] Arjun: How do costs look for dedicated with burst capacity? Do you do monthly committed slots?
[06:02] Lena: Dedicated is reserved capacity; you subscribe to a capacity plan and can configure burst bands. Pricing is a combination of reserved commit and overage/burst rates. Diego will prepare a cost estimate for your target profiles.
[06:15] Maya: Can you also show us an example of instrumented tracing and per-token cost breakdown in the console? We want to see token-level costs tied to routes.
[06:23] Diego: Absolutely. Our console has per-token cost, latency percentiles per route, and tracing hooks that show kernel-level timings. We'll include screenshots in the follow-up.
[06:33] Arjun: Any mentionable limitations with streaming and very long sequences? We have some long-form responses sometimes 2k-3k tokens.
[06:40] Diego: Long sequences change memory pressure and KV cache behaviour. For very long contexts, you might benefit from model sharding or offloading strategies; we'll test 2k-3k cases and report memory and p95 tradeoffs.
[06:55] Maya: For our compliance team, can you deliver SOC2 report and details on retention and audit logs?
[07:01] Lena: Yes, we'll attach SOC2 and the retention policy. Private also has audit log options.
[07:06] Tom: Also, if we use private deployment, how is software updates handled? We prefer controlled patch windows.
[07:12] Diego: Private supports scheduled updates controlled by customer; we push patches to a private control plane and you approve deploy windows.
[07:20] Arjun: Cool. Let's talk about the bench itself — what arrival patterns can your harness emulate? Bursty poisson, closed-loop?
[07:27] Diego: It supports Poisson, deterministic bursts, closed-loop (one-request-per-session), and custom traces. We can run your historical traffic as a trace replay.
[07:36] Maya: We need the harness to produce token/sec time-series and p95 moving window.
[07:40] Diego: Check — we'll output time-series and percentile curves and raw logs.
[07:45] Arjun: If the bench shows we can't meet 350ms p95 under hosted, is the typical move dedicated or do people optimize prompts?
[07:52] Lena: Both. Customers often tune prompt engineering (shorter prefixes), enable KV caching, or move to dedicated for guarantees. We recommend iterative approach: run hosted bench, tune, then consider dedicated if needed.
[08:05] Tom: For the bench run we'll need to run across our VPN endpoints. Is Redwood able to run tests from within our VPC?
[08:10] Diego: For private customers we can run in your VPC; for hosted, we can arrange agent-based in-region runners or private links to get accurate measurements.
[08:20] Maya: About analytics: will we get a breakdown of token cost per route and per model?
[08:24] Diego: Yes, console provides token-level cost allocation per API key and route; we'll give example exports.
[08:31] Arjun: Ok onto a nitty-gritty — your earlier estimate of 3-6k tokens/sec per GPU was broad. Can you give a small matrix for different concurrency targets?
[08:38] Diego: Sure — hypothetical numbers: low-latency streaming mode: 3k tokens/sec per A100 equiv; balanced mode: 6-9k tokens/sec; high-throughput (larger batch windows): 12-18k tokens/sec. These assume 250-token average output and quantized 13B model. We'll validate with runs.
[08:59] Maya: Makes sense. How long do warm-up periods take for KV cache to hit steady state?
[09:04] Diego: Dependent on request overlap; with heavy prefix repetition steady-state can be within minutes; we'll instrument warmup curves in the report.
[09:12] Arjun: On monitoring, can we get edge-to-edge traces (loadbalancer -> runtime -> GPU kernel times)?
[09:18] Diego: Yes — distributed tracing with span durations at kernel, runtime, and network boundaries.
[09:24] Tom: For capacity planning, what's your recommended safety margin for p95? 20% headroom?
[09:30] Diego: 20-30% is common for bursty workloads; dedicated autoscaling reduces need for large headroom if you have burst bands configured.
[09:38] Maya: If we set a strict p95 SLA, how do rollbacks or automatic fallbacks interact if a model update regresses latency?
[09:45] Lena: Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to prompt sets. You can configure automatic rollback policies if latency or quality regresses.
[09:52] Arjun: Great. Any differences in telemetry fidelity between hosted and private?
[09:58] Diego: Private can forward logs to your SIEM and keep higher fidelity traces, but hosted has rich built-in dashboards.
[10:05] Maya: Let's schedule the benchmarking window. We prefer mid-next-week, 2-4 hours so we can iterate.
[10:10] Lena: We'll propose two slots in the follow-up.
[10:13] Tom: For the benchmark, we'll need a stubbed traffic generator in our VPC. Can Redwood supply a runner we can deploy?
[10:18] Diego: Yes — a small agent you can run that replays traces and pushes traffic over private link. We'll hand you the runner image.
[10:25] Arjun: On fallback options — if we use dedicated with fallback to hosted in another region, how do you handle model parity?
[10:31] Diego: Model variants are pinned; we recommend keeping identical model artifacts across regions for parity. Smart routing only falls back to compatible variants; we maintain a model catalog with verified performance profiles.
[10:44] Maya: Any notion of per-token throttling during overload rather than dropping connections?
[10:49] Diego: You can set graceful degradation policies—throttle token rate, reduce max tokens, or fall back to smaller model.
[10:56] Arjun: That could help during sudden bursts.
[10:58] Lena: Ok let's recap next steps quickly.
[11:02] Diego: I'll run the bench plan and cost estimate.
[11:05] Lena: Lena will send benchmark plan and compliance docs.
[11:08] Maya: We'll upload prompt sets and network docs.
[11:11] Tom: I'll coordinate SRE availability for the bench.
[11:14] Arjun: We'll review the cost estimate and run the bench. If results look good we'll scope a dedicated pilot.
[11:21] Lena: Thanks everyone. We will follow up with the plan and two slots for the bench.
[11:26] Arjun: Thank you.
[11:28] Maya: Thanks all.
[11:30] Tom: Bye.
